one_line_contribution: An item-level partition of agent failures into coverage failures (gold never sampled) and selection failures (gold sampled but outvoted), used to (a) derive a measured 'recoverable-coverage ceiling' bounding what any memory bank can buy, (b) adjudicate agreement-gated memory against agreement-gated extra sampling at matched tokens, and (c) test whether an instruction optimizer and a self-editing memory repair near-disjoint item sets.
closest_prior_work: Two works the proposal never cites threaten it more than the ones it concedes. (1) Brown et al., 'Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling' (2024), and the verifier/reranking line it sits in (Cobbe et al. 2021; Li et al. 2023), already decompose repeated-sampling performance into exactly coverage (is the answer in the sample set) versus selection/verification (can you pick it), and already show coverage rising with n while selection lags. The proposal's E0 stratification is that decomposition with SOLVED split by vote share; presenting it as 'what survives as ours' is not sustainable once a reviewer names this line. (2) Mallen et al., 'When Not to Trust Language Models' (ACL 2023) established that retrieval augmentation *hurts* precisely the questions the model already answers confidently and gated retrieval on that basis; the proposal's signature mechanistic claim — 'injection's damage falls almost entirely on high-agreement already-solved items' — is the same finding with vote-share substituted for entity popularity, and the Self-RAG/FLARE/Adaptive-RAG citations given do not cover it. What remains genuinely unclaimed after these two, plus the conceded MemRL/MemDelta/Evo-Memory protocol collisions and the Adaptive-Consistency gate collision, is narrow: the AGM-vs-AGS control and the stratum-decomposed disjointness test in E7.
strongest_objection: The coverage/selection partition is not a property of the model or the item; it is a property of the base prompt, temperature and n used to label it, and both load-bearing claims are damaged by this. (i) The Short Hypothesis and Abstract assert that 'sampling and instruction edits can only convert selection failures' and that 'injected experience is the only mechanism that can convert coverage failures.' The first half is simply false: raising n raises coverage — that is what pass@k growth *is* — and the paper's own decisive competitor AGS spends its gated budget on additional memory-free samples, i.e. on the one intervention that most directly attacks COVERAGE-FAIL@8. So the mechanistic story predicts AGM > AGS for a reason the experiment disproves by construction, and pool A's own 24 rollouts will show COVERAGE-FAIL@8 items whose gold appears by n=16 or 24. The 'recoverable-coverage ceiling' is therefore a function of the sampling configuration used to define it, not a ceiling on memory, and P8's claim that the coverage stratum shrinks at 14B is confounded with the fact that a stronger model's stratum was labelled at the same fixed n=8 and T=0.7. (ii) In a *tool-using* ReAct agent, instruction edits change search queries, hop order and stopping behaviour, hence change which documents enter context and which answers are reachable at all. GEPA-optimized instructions can and routinely do manufacture answers that never appeared under the base prompt — that is a coverage fix, not a selection fix. P6 predicts INSTR's fixes are ≤15% COVERAGE-FAIL; for a retrieval agent the more likely outcome is the opposite, and because strata are labelled by the *base* memory-free agent, any INSTR fix on an item whose trajectory changed is scored against a reference frame that no longer describes that condition. Either way the 'division of labour' theory is not identified by E7: a pass is partly definitional (strata frozen at the base prompt), and a failure is over-determined by the agentic setting rather than informative about instructions vs. memory. Secondary, but it will be raised: the study pre-commits to a bounded null in the one regime the proposal itself argues is most favourable to sampling (short factoid answers where majority vote is well defined), while explicitly scoping out the long-horizon procedural tasks where ExpeL/Reflexion/ReasoningBank actually claim their wins — so a null here does not qualify the literature it is aimed at.
what_would_fix_it: Four concrete changes, roughly in order of importance. (1) Stop treating strata as fixed labels and report the coverage-conversion matrix: label each item's stratum at every budget point n ∈ {8,16,24} from pool A, publish coverage@n saturation curves, and state the recoverable-coverage ceiling as a function of n rather than a scalar. If the ceiling collapses when n rises to the AGS budget, that is the paper's real result and it should be the headline, not a footnote. It costs nothing — pool A already contains the rollouts. (2) Re-label strata per condition as well as by the base agent for E7, and report both frames; specifically report, for INSTR, how many fixes are items whose *retrieval trajectory* changed, since those are coverage fixes attributable to instructions and they directly test the theory's central asymmetry. (3) Add the two omitted arms named below. (4) Actually run the committed literature search before claiming novelty, and drop or heavily requalify P2's mechanism as a replication of Mallen-style 'retrieval harms what the model already knows' at the vote-share level rather than a new finding. Optionally, add one procedural/agentic task with a verifier-based best-of-n aggregation so the null, if it comes, is not confined to the regime where nobody claimed memory wins.
missing_baseline: Two. (a) **Agreement-gated extra retrieval (AGR)** — on the same low-agreement items and at matched tokens, spend the gated budget on more search calls, query reformulation, or a larger retrieval top-k instead of on injected experience. In multi-hop QA over a local index, a coverage failure is usually a failed bridge-entity retrieval, so this is the obvious and much cheaper way to convert coverage failures. Without it, even a clean AGM > AGS win cannot support 'injected experience is the only mechanism that converts coverage failures' — the paper would have shown only that memory beats *more samples*, not that it beats *more retrieval*. Its absence is the single clearest hole in E3, whose baseline list runs to six arms and omits the one that attacks the same stratum. (b) **An optimizer-selected demonstration baseline** (MIPRO / DSPy bootstrapped few-shot with random search over demonstration slots, fixed at test time, no self-editing). The track's framing is 'optimizer owns instructions, memory owns demonstrations'; E7 deliberately fits the instruction slot only, which means the demonstration slot is only ever occupied by retrieved memory. Pool D (retrieved solved exemplars) is not a substitute — it is retrieval-based, not optimizer-selected. Without a static optimized-demonstration arm, P6's disjointness result cannot distinguish 'memory is doing something instructions cannot' from 'demonstrations are doing something instructions cannot, and any demonstration source would do'.
preprint_collision: The check is, by its own admission, empty: the search tool hit a session-wide usage limit and returned no results, so this round contributes zero new evidence and the positioning is explicitly carried over and 'unverified as of now'. The proposal deserves credit for refusing to launder the failure into a novelty claim, and for having already demoted two claims (compute-matching, free gate) after earlier searches — that is more honest than most submissions. But honesty about an unsearched claim does not make it searched: as submitted, novelty is asserted, not established, and the commitment to search 'before submission' is exactly the work a reviewer is being asked to take on faith. Concretely, the carried-over list is also incomplete in ways a working search would likely have caught: it names no coverage-vs-selection decomposition from the repeated-sampling literature (Large Language Monkeys and successors), and no popularity/confidence-gated retrieval work showing retrieval harms already-known items (Mallen et al. 2023; SKR; the self-knowledge-gated RAG line), which is the nearest prior statement of the proposal's own P2 mechanism. The proposed query list also omits the terms most likely to surface a collision — 'coverage vs precision repeated sampling', 'when does retrieval hurt', 'confidence-gated retrieval', 'pass@k maj@k gap' — and searches only for memory-framed phrasings of a claim whose closest relatives are phrased in sampling and RAG terms. I score this as a weakness, not a neutral: the two surviving contributions (AGM-vs-AGS, stratum-level disjointness) are plausibly novel to me, but that is my prior, not the proposal's evidence.
